questions.prompt: Cinderline wants a nightly job that labels 40,000 free-text work-order notes as electrical, hydraulic or mechanical and stores the label in a column. Which building block fits the shape of this work?

options.text: A task-specific AI Function such as ai_classify inside a scheduled SQL query.
options.rationale: Correct: one model call per row, labels supplied in the query and the result written as a column; no agent logic is needed.

options.text: A Supervisor Agent that routes each note to a tool.
options.rationale: Routing serves interactive requests that need a choice of tool; a fixed labelling job has no choice to make.

options.text: A Knowledge Assistant over the work-order table.
options.rationale: A Knowledge Assistant answers questions from documents; it does not write a label into every row of a table.

options.text: A provisioned-throughput endpoint on its own.
options.rationale: Provisioned throughput is capacity, not logic; something would still have to loop over the rows and call it.

questions.prompt: Which observation most directly argues for moving Cinderline's assistant from a pay-per-token endpoint to provisioned throughput?

options.text: Production traffic is steady, and load tests at the expected peak were refused by the pay-per-token endpoint's limits.
options.rationale: Correct: predictable production volume plus evidence that shared limits cannot carry the peak is the case for reserved capacity.

options.text: The team wants to compare three different models this week.
options.rationale: Trying several models favours pay-per-token, which needs no sizing and charges nothing for idle capacity.

options.text: The assistant receives a few dozen questions a day.
options.rationale: Low, irregular volume would leave reserved capacity idle; per-token charging fits it better.

options.text: A launch announcement says a larger model is now available.
options.rationale: An announcement is not evidence about Cinderline's volume, limits or regional availability.

questions.prompt: An analyst joins work_order_notes to assets before calling ai_query, and the join repeats each note three times because each work order lists three assets. What happens to the model calls?

options.text: They triple: the function runs once per joined row, so identical note text is sent three times.
options.rationale: Correct: the function is evaluated for every row that reaches it; deduplicating notes before the call removes two thirds of the calls.

options.text: They stay the same because the engine sends each distinct prompt only once.
options.rationale: No such deduplication is documented; assume every row that reaches the function is a call.

options.text: They stay the same because AI Functions run before joins.
options.rationale: Expressions in the select list are evaluated on the joined rows; the join happens first.

options.text: They fall, because a join lets the endpoint batch similar requests.
options.rationale: Batching can affect throughput at best; it does not reduce the number of rows the function is applied to.

questions.prompt: The Knowledge Assistant answers correctly in its author's session, but the technicians' tablet app gets a permission error on every call. What should the platform owner check first?

options.text: Whether the app's identity holds CAN_QUERY on the assistant and its endpoint.
options.rationale: Correct: a refusal before any answer points to the caller's permission, and the author's own access proves nothing about the app's identity.

options.text: Whether the endpoint has enough provisioned capacity.
options.rationale: Capacity problems slow or throttle requests; they do not produce a permission error on every call.

options.text: Whether the assistant's instructions mention the tablet app.
options.rationale: Instructions shape answers after a request is accepted; they cannot grant access to anyone.

options.text: Whether the manuals volume has been synced since the last upload.
options.rationale: Stale sources give outdated answers; the app is not getting answers at all.

questions.prompt: Service bulletin SB-114 revision D was copied into the manuals volume this morning, yet the assistant still quotes revision C. What is the first thing to check?

options.text: The files source's state and knowledge cutoff time, then run a sync of the non-index sources.
options.rationale: Correct: a cutoff earlier than the copy means revision D was never ingested, and syncing is how files sources are brought up to date.

options.text: Whether the endpoint needs more provisioned throughput.
options.rationale: Capacity affects speed and throttling; it cannot make the assistant aware of a file it never ingested.

options.text: Add an instruction telling the assistant to prefer the newest revision.
options.rationale: Instructions shape answers from ingested content; they cannot surface a file that was never ingested.

options.text: Delete and recreate the assistant.
options.rationale: Recreating is slow and loses configuration; the source's state and cutoff already point to a cheaper, targeted fix.

questions.prompt: Which evaluation case would have caught the failure in the second state before release?

options.text: A labelled two-part question whose expectations name stock_lookup as a required tool, checked with a tool-call scorer.
options.rationale: Correct: it encodes the routing expectation directly, so an answer drawn only from the manuals fails even when it reads well.

options.text: A question answerable from a single manual.
options.rationale: It exercises retrieval, not routing; the supervisor would pass it without ever needing the stock tool.

options.text: A latency test at peak load.
options.rationale: The wrong answer was fast and fluent; latency says nothing about which tool was chosen.

options.text: Swapping in a larger foundation model.
options.rationale: That is a change to try, not an evaluation case; without a case nobody would know whether it fixed routing.

questions.prompt: Given the labelled mix in the visual, what is the strongest reason for Cinderline's first release to use retrieval over the manuals rather than a Supervisor Agent?

options.text: 52 of 60 questions need only the manuals, so a routing step would add a failure point and extra calls to nearly every question to serve eight.
options.rationale: Correct: the labelled mix is the evidence, and the routing tax falls on every question while its benefit reaches only eight.

options.text: Supervisor Agents cannot call Knowledge Assistants.
options.rationale: The SDK lists knowledge_assistant as a supervisor tool type, so this is false and cannot be the reason.

options.text: Fixed retrieval workflows cannot produce wrong answers.
options.rationale: They can retrieve the wrong passage or cite badly; fixed steps make failures countable, not impossible.

options.text: Supervisor Agents are newer, so they should wait for a later release.
options.rationale: Age is not a criterion in either direction; the question mix is the evidence that decides.

questions.prompt: Cinderline's assistant answers a plant-2 technician with a bulletin that only plant-3 staff may see. Whose control failed first?

options.text: Cinderline's governance: the assistant's sources held plant-3 bulletins for everyone who can query it.
options.rationale: Correct: hosting worked as designed; what the assistant can retrieve is set by the sources and grants Cinderline configured.

options.text: Databricks' hosting of the serving compute.
options.rationale: Compute ran the request as configured; hosting does not decide which documents are in the sources.

options.text: The pay-per-token model's training data.
options.rationale: The bulletin came from Cinderline's own sources through retrieval, not from the model's training.

options.text: The AI Gateway rate limit.
options.rationale: A rate limit caps volume; it never decides which documents a caller may see.

questions.prompt: A launch post says 'Knowledge Assistant is now available to all customers.' Which cell of Cinderline's availability table can you fill from it?

options.text: None; record the post as a lead and verify stage, region and workspace enablement in current documentation and in the workspace.
options.rationale: Correct: an announcement is not a dated statement about Cinderline's cloud, region or workspace, so those cells stay unknown until checked.

options.text: Cloud and region: available, because it says all customers.
options.rationale: Availability varies by cloud and region; an announcement cannot establish it for a specific account.

options.text: Release stage: GA, because it says available.
options.rationale: The provider page read in this build labels the resource Public Beta; wording in a post does not set a stage.

options.text: Parity: the same on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.
options.rationale: Cross-cloud parity must be checked in each documentation set; nothing in a post proves it.

questions.prompt: In the second state the Knowledge Assistant has the higher average correctness. Under the rules agreed before the run, what decides the release?

options.text: Neither candidate is eligible yet: the Knowledge Assistant fails the refusal rule on Q33 and the fixed workflow fails the superseded-revision rule on Q19.
options.rationale: Correct: both rules were agreed before results, and each candidate breaks one; exposing another plant's bulletin and citing a superseded manual are failures no average can offset.

options.text: The Knowledge Assistant, for its higher average correctness, 0.90 against 0.85.
options.rationale: Averages rank candidates but hide which cases failed; the refusal rule was agreed to prevent exactly this trade, and Q33 breaks it.

options.text: The fixed workflow, because only a refusal failure blocks and Q19 is a quality miss.
options.rationale: Citing revision A where revision B is current breaks the agreed superseded-revision rule, the retrieval module's zero-superseded pass bar, so it blocks just as Q33 does.

options.text: Whichever candidate is newer.
options.rationale: Release date is not an evaluation result and appears in no agreed rule.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline's security lead asks: 'If we route an external model through a Databricks serving endpoint, does retrieved manual text stay inside Databricks?' Answer precisely and say what you would verify before the design review.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: No. The endpoint centralizes access, permissions, AI Gateway controls and logging, but its served entity forwards the whole prompt, including any retrieved manual text, to the provider, which processes it under Cinderline's provider account. Because security forbids that for manual content, the manual-answering path should use a Databricks-hosted pay-per-token or provisioned endpoint. Before the review I would verify the provider's data-handling terms, whether external models remain allowed for public text, and which hosted models and modes are available in Cinderline's region.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The answer separates what the endpoint controls from where the model runs, applies the stated rule, and turns provider terms and availability into checks rather than assumptions. Mentioning a masking guardrail as a partial mitigation is acceptable if its limits are stated.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline plans to deploy its assistant as an agent endpoint and rely on AI Gateway PII guardrails and per-user rate limits there. What do you tell the platform owner, citing which artifact, and where would you put those controls instead?
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0, dated 2026-09-23, says agent endpoints currently support only inference tables among AI Gateway features, and databricks-agents 1.12.0 configures only an inference table on deploy, so PII guardrails and per-user rate limits cannot be assumed on the agent endpoint. Put rate limits and guardrails on the pay-per-token or provisioned endpoint the agent calls, remove personal data from documents before they are indexed, grant CAN_QUERY only to the technicians' app identity, and re-check the current documentation before the design review.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The answer quotes an artifact and date instead of a general claim, moves each control to a layer that supports it, and leaves the status open to re-verification. Enforcing limits in the calling application is an acceptable alternative if it is tested.

selfQuestions.prompt: Name two Cinderline requirements that would justify a custom agent over a Knowledge Assistant, and two ongoing costs the team accepts by choosing it.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Justifying requirements: answers must cite manual, revision and page in a fixed format that the assistant's instructions cannot guarantee, and retrieval must always try the newest manual revision before service bulletins. Accepted costs: the team maintains and pins the code and its dependencies and redeploys it (in its Databricks App, or through the agent framework on the legacy endpoint path), and it must run the evaluation set and inspect traces on every change, because no platform pipeline tests the custom logic for it.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Each justification is a requirement the configured agent cannot express, not a preference, and each cost is recurring work that follows from owning the code. A tool that must run as a specific service principal, or a deterministic refusal rule, are equally valid justifications.

selfQuestions.prompt: A colleague argues that the Supervisor Agent is the newest and most capable pattern, so it should be Cinderline's default. Rebut the argument with two criteria from the decision table and say what evidence would change your mind.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Capability is not the requirement. On risk, the supervisor adds a routing decision to every question, with wrong-tool and denied-tool failures, while 46 of 60 labelled questions need only the manuals. On evaluation, it needs tool-call cases and per-tool permission tests before release that the first release does not otherwise need. I would change my mind if stock or work-order questions reached about one in five of real questions, or if answers had to use live stock data.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The rebuttal uses the table's criteria and the labelled mix instead of opinion, and states a measurable switching condition. Operations, with more tools to maintain, is an equally valid criterion to cite.

selfQuestions.prompt: Without using any price, explain how Cinderline's daily model calls change if the assistant moves from a fixed retrieval workflow to a Supervisor Agent, and what you would measure after a pilot to replace the assumption.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: At 300 questions a day the fixed workflow makes about two steps per question, roughly 600 calls; a supervisor with one routing step, one or two tool calls and one generation makes three or four, roughly 900 to 1,200 calls, and every question pays the routing step. After a pilot I would read the usage-tracking system tables for the endpoints, count steps per question in the traces, attribute costs through endpoint tags and apply the rates from current pricing on that day.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The answer multiplies drivers before any rate, shows that the routing tax applies to every question, and names the measurement sources that replace the assumption. Estimating tokens per step instead of calls is an acceptable variant.

beats.title: Who writes the logic above the model decides the building block
beats.outcome: Place a proposed AI feature on the building-block map by asking who writes the logic between the request and the model.
beats.explanation: Managed AI on Databricks is several [[dbxfe-ai-platform-blocks-concept|building blocks]], not one product. Foundation-model access gives you a model behind an endpoint and nothing else. AI Functions put a model call inside a SQL query. Agent Bricks agents, such as a Knowledge Assistant, are configured rather than coded. A custom agent is your own code, which Databricks developer documentation now recommends running in a Databricks App; deploying it to its own serving endpoint is the legacy path. Notice in the second state that one technician question lands on a different block depending on who writes the retrieval: the platform, a SQL author or your team.

handbook.markdown:
Read the map as a question about who owns the logic, then about hosting.

| Block | Who writes the logic | What you configure | Typical request |
|---|---|---|---|
| Foundation-model access | Your application | Endpoint, prompt, parameters | One chat or embedding call |
| AI Functions | A SQL author | The query, labels or schema, the endpoint for `ai_query` | One model call per row |
| Agent Bricks agent | The platform, from your configuration | Knowledge sources, tools, instructions, examples | One question; retrieval or routing inside |
| Custom agent | Your team's code | Everything, run in a Databricks App or, on the legacy path, deployed with the agent framework | One question; your own steps |

Databricks developer documentation uses Agent Bricks as the name of its whole agent platform, custom Python agents included; in this map an Agent Bricks agent means a configured one, such as a Knowledge Assistant or Supervisor Agent.

Three services sit across all four. Model Serving hosts the endpoints on Databricks-managed serverless compute. The AI Gateway governs traffic on those endpoints. MLflow records traces and runs evaluations.

The Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0, read in this build, names matching client services: `serving_endpoints`, `ai_functions`, `knowledge_assistants`, `supervisor_agents`, `agent_bricks` (the Custom LLM product) and a Unity Catalog `ai_gateway`. Console labels can differ, and a client service existing does not mean it is enabled in any workspace.

Two mistakes recur. The first is choosing by model: the same model can sit behind every block, so its name decides nothing about ownership. The second is choosing by novelty: a newer block usually decides more for you, which helps only when those decisions match your requirements. To explain the map to a customer honestly, take three of their real requests, place each on it, and say for each who would debug a wrong answer.

beats.recap: Ask who writes the logic above the model; the answer names the block.
beats.changeNote: Corrected how this beat describes hosting a custom agent: it had said a custom agent is hosted on a serving endpoint. Databricks developer documentation (devhub commit 35f4745, custom agents page) recommends a Databricks App and calls deploying it to its own endpoint a legacy path. The handbook also says which agents this map calls Agent Bricks agents, following the overview page.

beats.title: Per-token access rents calls; provisioned throughput reserves capacity
beats.outcome: Choose between pay-per-token and provisioned-throughput access from a workload's volume, predictability and model needs, without quoting a price.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-ai-platform-payg-concept|Pay-per-token]] endpoints are Databricks-hosted and charge for the tokens each request uses, so a quiet day costs little and a busy one consumes more within the endpoint's limits. [[dbxfe-ai-platform-throughput-concept|Provisioned throughput]] reserves capacity for one model, sized in model units with optional burst scaling, and its charge follows the capacity kept provisioned. Notice in the tables that the same weekly token total arrives evenly in one week and in a burst in the other; the rate column stays empty because prices are read on the day.

samajh.text: Socho aapke phone ke do plan hain. Ek prepaid top-up jahan har GB ka paisa lagta hai: kam use kiya to kam bill, par network busy ho to speed ki koi guarantee nahi. Doosra fixed monthly plan jiski speed tay hai: mahine bhar paisa lagega chahe phone drawer mein pada rahe. Kaunsa sasta hai, woh aapke use ke pattern pe depend karta hai, plan ke naam pe nahi.
samajh.mapping: The per-GB top-up is pay-per-token billing for tokens used; the fixed monthly plan with a set speed is provisioned throughput charged for capacity kept provisioned.
samajh.boundary: Provisioned throughput reserves capacity for one model and can burst beyond it; its units, limits and rates come from current documentation and pricing, not from a phone plan.

handbook.markdown:
Both modes serve Databricks-hosted foundation models through serving endpoints; they differ in what you are charged for and what is guaranteed.

**Pay-per-token.** Endpoints for supported models are available without sizing anything; each request consumes input and output tokens, and the charge follows those tokens. Endpoint limits apply, so a load test can hit them long before a budget does. As previously read in the Foundation Model APIs documentation, this is the mode for getting started, for experiments and for lower or variable volume.

**Provisioned throughput.** You create an endpoint for one model and size it. In the Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 a provisioned-throughput served entity takes `provisioned_model_units`, and `burst_scaling_enabled`, on by default, lets the endpoint scale beyond provisioned capacity; with it off, capacity stays fixed. Older served-entity fields express capacity as minimum and maximum tokens per second. The Terraform provider v1.133.0 example sizes a model from the `system.ai` catalog with `provisioned_model_units = 100`. The documentation positions this mode for production workloads that need predictable performance.

```text
Synthetic sizing note (no prices)
steady week: 5.1 million tokens, peak day about 1.05 million
burst week:  5.1 million tokens, peak day about 4.1 million
ask: can pay-per-token limits carry the peak day?
ask: would provisioned capacity sit idle four days in five?
```

What to inspect: the endpoint's usage in the usage-tracking system tables when the AI Gateway's usage tracking is enabled, the peak rather than the average, and whether a refused request was a limit or an error. What this beat does not settle: which models each mode offers in your region, and the rates. Both are read from current documentation and pricing on the day of the decision.

beats.recap: Pay-per-token charges for tokens used; provisioned throughput charges for capacity kept; the workload's shape decides.

beats.title: An external model endpoint moves the data boundary, not only the bill
beats.outcome: Explain what an external model endpoint centralizes and what it hands to the provider, and decide when a security rule excludes it.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-ai-platform-external-concept|external model endpoint]] is a serving endpoint whose served entity forwards each request to a provider such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud Vertex AI, using a key referenced from a secret scope. Callers get one Databricks endpoint, its permissions and its AI Gateway controls. The prompt, including any manual text retrieved into it, still travels to the provider, which processes it under your provider account. Notice in the second state that Cinderline's rule removes this option for manual content only.

handbook.markdown:
In the Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 an external model is a served entity with a `provider`, a model `name`, a `task` and a provider-specific configuration. The provider values listed are `ai21labs`, `anthropic`, `amazon-bedrock`, `cohere`, `databricks-model-serving`, `google-cloud-vertex-ai`, `openai`, `palm` and `custom`. The Terraform provider v1.133.0 example keeps the key out of code:

```hcl
external_model {
  name     = "gpt-4o-mini"
  provider = "openai"
  task     = "llm/v1/chat"
  openai_config {
    openai_api_key = "{{secrets/llm_scope/openai_api_key}}"
  }
}
```

The same page says that when an external model is present the endpoint can have only one served entity, and that an endpoint cannot later be converted to or from an external model. The SDK 0.141.0 docstring for the same field, two days newer, repeats the conversion rule but says instead that all external models within an endpoint must share one task type, which implies several may share an endpoint. Decide at creation whether an endpoint serves external models; how many it may hold is a question for current documentation, because the two artifacts disagree.

What the endpoint gives you: one URL and permission model for callers, AI Gateway controls on the traffic, usage tracking, and payload logging into your Unity Catalog. What it does not give you: control over where the model runs, what the provider retains, or the provider's own limits and charges, which apply under your provider account. Any Databricks-side charge for the endpoint is a current-pricing question.

Diagnose by layer. A permission error comes from the Databricks endpoint before the provider is called; an authentication failure from the provider usually means the secret holds the wrong key; a limit can be enforced by the gateway or by the provider, so record which one refused the request. A newer Unity Catalog surface, the model provider service, stores provider credentials as a governed securable; the AI Gateway beat's extension card covers it.

beats.recap: An external endpoint centralizes access and controls; the prompt still goes to the provider.
beats.changeNote: Corrected this beat's teaching on external-model endpoints: it had presented the Terraform provider v1.133.0's one-served-entity rule as a fixed limit. The Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 reference (serving.py, commit 9df82c7) says instead that external models in one endpoint must share a task type, so both statements are now attributed and the one-endpoint-per-model advice is removed.

beats.title: AI Functions put one model call on every row
beats.outcome: Read a SQL query that calls a model per row and predict what drives its call count, cost and failures.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-ai-platform-aiquery-concept|ai_query]] sends each row's request to a serving endpoint you name, from inside a SQL query, so a table of 40,000 notes becomes 40,000 model calls. [[dbxfe-ai-platform-taskfn-concept|Task-specific functions]] such as ai_classify and ai_extract fix the task and the managed model: you pass text plus labels or a schema. Notice in the second state that the new column is computed per row like any expression, and that a blank note yields no usable label, so decide before the run whether such rows are filtered out, reviewed or allowed to fail the query.

handbook.markdown:
AI Functions come in two shapes.

**Task-specific functions** fix the task. In the Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 their REST equivalents are `ai_classify` (content plus 2 to 500 labels, or labels mapped to descriptions), `ai_extract` (content plus a schema of fields) and `ai_parse_document` (a document in a Unity Catalog volume, such as a PDF). As previously read in the AI Functions documentation, SQL also offers functions such as `ai_summarize`, `ai_translate` and `ai_analyze_sentiment`.

**`ai_query`** is general-purpose: you name a serving endpoint (a pay-per-token model, a provisioned-throughput endpoint, an external model or your own model) and pass the request.

```sql
-- Synthetic tables; run on a sample before a full run.
SELECT note_id,
       ai_classify(note_text, ARRAY('electrical', 'hydraulic', 'mechanical')) AS fault_family
FROM cinderline.maintenance.work_order_notes
WHERE note_date >= DATE'2026-09-01'
LIMIT 200;

SELECT note_id,
       ai_query('cinderline-summaries',
                CONCAT('Summarize the fault in one sentence: ', note_text)) AS summary
FROM cinderline.maintenance.work_order_notes
LIMIT 200;
```

Reason about it as SQL. The function is an expression evaluated for every row that reaches it, so filters shrink the call count and joins can multiply it: classify distinct notes first, then join the labels. Keep the prompt stable so re-runs are comparable, write results to a table rather than recomputing them in dashboards, and record which endpoint and which date produced a column.

What fails: rows the model cannot handle (empty or oversized text), rate limits on large runs, and an endpoint the query's identity may not use. The current reference describes signatures, error-handling options, supported compute and regional availability; read it before relying on any of them. When not to use it: interactive, multi-step questions belong to an agent, and a deterministic rule, such as a keyword in a code field, belongs in plain SQL.

beats.recap: One row reaching the function is one model call; filter and deduplicate before you call.

beats.title: An agent is served like a model: version, endpoint, route, permission
beats.outcome: Trace how a custom or Agent Bricks agent becomes a queryable endpoint, and name the permission a caller needs.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-ai-platform-endpoint-concept|Model Serving]] exposes a model or agent it serves as a REST endpoint on Databricks-managed serverless compute that does not appear in your cloud account. An endpoint holds served entities and traffic routes, and callers need CAN_QUERY. For a custom agent on the legacy path, the agent framework's deploy() takes a Unity Catalog model version, creates or updates the [[dbxfe-ai-platform-agentendpoint-concept|agent endpoint]] with an inference table and routes all traffic to that version. Notice in the second state that version 2 stays served at zero traffic after version 3 is deployed.

handbook.markdown:
The Serving Endpoints API in the Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 describes endpoints as scalable REST endpoints on serverless compute, fully managed by Databricks and not appearing in the customer's cloud account. An endpoint serves up to ten served entities, and a traffic configuration splits requests among them by percentage. Permission levels are CAN_VIEW, CAN_QUERY and CAN_MANAGE.

On the legacy path, which Databricks developer documentation now says to replace by running the agent in a Databricks App, a custom agent reaches an endpoint in four steps, sketched with synthetic names:

```python
import mlflow
from databricks import agents

mlflow.set_experiment("/Shared/cinderline-manuals-agent")  # traces go here
info = mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(
    name="manuals_agent",
    python_model="agent.py",  # a ResponsesAgent defined in code
    registered_model_name="cinderline.maintenance.manuals_agent",
)
agents.deploy("cinderline.maintenance.manuals_agent", info.registered_model_version)
```

In databricks-agents 1.12.0, `deploy()` creates the endpoint when it does not exist, with an AI Gateway inference table in the model's catalog and schema; sets tracing to an experiment it can find, or warns that there is none; and on a redeploy adds the new version with 100 percent of traffic while earlier versions stay served at 0 percent. `scale_to_zero` defaults to off, so check what older versions cost before leaving them in place, and remember the ten-entity limit.

Agent Bricks agents skip these steps: a Knowledge Assistant or Supervisor Agent reports its own `endpoint_name`. Either way, the caller's identity needs CAN_QUERY. Troubleshoot in order: permission (the request is refused before any agent code runs), endpoint state (a failed build or an update still in progress), then the agent's own logic in its traces.

beats.recap: Deploying moves a route and keeps old versions served; callers still need CAN_QUERY.
beats.changeNote: Clarified this beat: it no longer says every agent becomes a serving endpoint, and it labels the agents.deploy() steps as the legacy path for custom agents, following Databricks developer documentation (devhub commit 35f4745, custom agents page). The description of what deploy() configures is unchanged.

beats.title: AI Gateway controls depend on the endpoint type they sit on
beats.outcome: List what the AI Gateway can enforce and record, and state which endpoint types support each feature according to a named, dated artifact.
beats.explanation: The [[dbxfe-ai-platform-gateway-concept|AI Gateway]] settings on a serving endpoint can enforce rate limits per endpoint, user, group or service principal, apply input and output [[dbxfe-ai-platform-guardrail-concept|guardrails]] such as PII blocking, record usage in system tables and log payloads to an [[dbxfe-ai-platform-inference-concept|inference table]]. The Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 adds a condition: external-model, provisioned-throughput and pay-per-token endpoints are fully supported, while agent endpoints currently support only inference tables. Notice in the third state that the Terraform provider page states an older, narrower scope, so every cell carries its source and date.

handbook.markdown:
The Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 models the serving-endpoint AI Gateway as one configuration with five parts:

| Part | What it does | Where results appear |
|---|---|---|
| `rate_limits` | Caps calls or tokens per minute; key `endpoint` (default), `user`, `user_group` or `service_principal` | Refused requests |
| `guardrails` | Input and output filters: `safety`, `pii` (BLOCK, MASK or NONE), `invalid_keywords`, `valid_topics` | Blocked or masked content |
| `usage_tracking_config` | Records operational usage and associated costs | System tables |
| `inference_table_config` | Logs request and response payloads | A Unity Catalog table |
| `fallback_config` | Tries other served entities when one returns certain errors | The response |

A Terraform provider v1.133.0 example sets 10 calls per minute on the endpoint key, an inference table in `ml.ai_gateway`, and PII guardrails set to BLOCK on input and output.

Now the context that decides a design. The SDK's note says external-model, provisioned-throughput and pay-per-token endpoints are fully supported and agent endpoints currently support only inference tables; databricks-agents 1.12.0 matches it, since `deploy()` configures only an inference table. So per-user limits and PII guardrails cannot be assumed on an agent endpoint today: put them on the model endpoints the agent calls, filter documents before they are indexed, and keep CAN_QUERY narrow.

The Terraform page is older in places: it says only external model endpoints are supported, marks keyword and topic guardrails deprecated and says PII supports only BLOCK. When artifacts disagree, quote each with its version and date, prefer the current product documentation, and test in the workspace.

A second surface shares the name: the SDK's Unity Catalog `ai_gateway` service manages model services as governed securables. An extension card covers it; it is not the endpoint configuration above.

beats.recap: Gateway features are real; which endpoint types they cover is a dated statement from a named artifact.

beats.title: A Knowledge Assistant is configured from sources, instructions and examples
beats.outcome: Describe what you supply to a Knowledge Assistant, what the platform creates, and what must be synced when manuals change.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-ai-platform-knowledge-concept|Knowledge Assistant]] is an [[dbxfe-ai-platform-bricks-concept|Agent Bricks]] agent you configure rather than code. You give it a description, optional instructions and knowledge sources: a vector search index with text and document-link columns, files in a Unity Catalog volume, or a table holding file content. The platform creates an agent endpoint and an MLflow experiment. Notice the third state: a revised bulletin copied into the volume is not in the assistant's knowledge until the files source is synced; an index source follows its index instead.

samajh.text: Naye technician ko pehle din ek binder diya jaata hai: machine ke manuals, ek chhota note ki jawab kaise dena hai, aur kuch purane sawal-jawab examples ke liye. Woh binder dekh ke batata hai. Agar aaj manual ka naya revision aaya aur kisi ne binder mein page nahi badla, to woh purana torque value hi batayega, poore confidence ke saath.
samajh.mapping: The binder is the knowledge sources, the note is the instructions, the sample questions are the examples, and replacing the page is syncing the files source.
samajh.boundary: The assistant retrieves passages and generates an answer rather than reading like a person, and an index source is only as current as its own index, which keeps its own sync schedule.

handbook.markdown:
The Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 describes the configuration contract.

| You supply | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Name and purpose | `display_name`, `description` | Required on create; the name is unique in the workspace |
| Behaviour | `instructions` | Optional global instructions |
| Knowledge | knowledge sources | `index` (vector search index, text column, document-URI column), `files` (a Unity Catalog volume path), `file_table` (a table with a binary file column) |
| Expected behaviour | examples | A question and optional guidelines |
| Access | permissions | CAN_QUERY to use, CAN_MANAGE to change |

The platform returns an `endpoint_name` (the knowledge assistant agent endpoint), an `experiment_id` (its MLflow experiment) and a `state` of CREATING, ACTIVE or FAILED, with `error_info` on failure. Each knowledge source reports UPDATING, UPDATED or FAILED_UPDATE and a knowledge cutoff time before which content is being ingested. `sync_knowledge_sources` syncs all non-index sources; index sources are not synced by the assistant. An index source is only as fresh as its index: a TRIGGERED Delta Sync index still answers from the rows it held at its last sync, so for a stale answer from the bulletin index check its sync mode and last sync time ([the retrieval module's third clock](#/module/dbxfe-retrieval/dbxfe-retrieval-freshness)).

Worked diagnosis: a technician gets revision C of SB-114 after revision D was copied at 09:10. Read the files source: UPDATED with a cutoff of 07:00, so revision D was never ingested. Run the sync, wait for UPDATED, ask again. If the answer still cites revision C, check whether revision C is also still in the volume; two revisions side by side is a document-control problem that retrieval cannot solve.

What you do not control: chunking, retrieval and prompt assembly are the platform's. That is the point, and the limit: if Cinderline needs a retrieval order or citation format that instructions cannot produce, that is a reason for a custom agent. Whether answers respect each technician's own document permissions must be verified in current documentation; until then, scope the sources so that everyone who can query the assistant may see all of them. The Terraform provider v1.133.0 page for this resource carries a Public Beta badge; the status beat explains what that does and does not establish.

beats.recap: Configure sources, instructions and examples; sync files sources when documents change.

beats.title: A Supervisor Agent chooses among tools, and every choice can be wrong
beats.outcome: Explain how a Supervisor Agent routes a request among configured tools and name the failure modes that routing adds.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-ai-platform-supervisor-concept|Supervisor Agent]] is an Agent Bricks agent that decides, per request, which configured tool to call: a Knowledge Assistant, a Genie Agent (formerly Genie space), a Unity Catalog function, an MCP connection, an app or another supervisor, among the types SDK 0.141.0 lists. That is [[dbxfe-ai-platform-autonomy-concept|autonomous tool selection]]. More questions become answerable, and every request gains a routing decision that can pick the wrong tool, reach a tool the caller may not use, or call tools needlessly. Notice the second state: a stock question sent only to the manuals gets a fluent, wrong answer.

samajh.text: Hospital ki reception desk socho. Patient bolta hai 'seene mein dard hai aur purani report bhi leni hai'. Receptionist decide karta hai: ek kaam OPD ka, doosra lab counter ka. Achha receptionist dono jagah bhejta hai; thaka hua receptionist sirf OPD bhej deta hai aur report ka sawal wahin reh jaata hai. Aur agar lab counter band ho, to sahi jawab hai 'abhi nahi mil sakti', koi andaaza nahi.
samajh.mapping: The receptionist is the supervisor, each counter is a configured tool, sending the patient only to OPD is a wrong-tool route, and a closed counter is a denied tool call.
samajh.boundary: A supervisor's routing is generated per request by a model rather than learned from experience, and each tool call runs with an identity whose permissions must be verified.

handbook.markdown:
The Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 lets a Supervisor Agent hold tools of these types: `genie_space` (a Genie Agent), `knowledge_assistant`, `uc_function`, `uc_connection` (an external MCP server), `uc_mcp`, `app` (a custom MCP server or custom agent built as a Databricks app), `volume`, `dashboard`, `serving_endpoint`, `table`, `vector_search_index`, `catalog`, `schema`, `supervisor_agent`, `databricks_web_search` and `skill`. Each tool carries a description; the supervisor uses descriptions and instructions to decide. Like a Knowledge Assistant it reports an `endpoint_name` and an MLflow `experiment_id`, and takes examples with guidelines.

Routing is where the new failures live:

| Failure | What the user sees | How to catch it |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong tool | A fluent answer from the wrong source | Labelled questions naming the expected tool |
| Missing tool call | One part of a two-part question ignored | Multi-part questions in the set |
| Denied tool | An error or, worse, a guess | Cases run as a user without the grant |
| Unneeded calls | Latency and cost with no gain | Tool calls per question counted in traces |

A **Genie Agent** (formerly Genie space; the Genie API still identifies one by its space ID, and the supervisor tool type is still `genie_space`) is set up by analysts so that business users can ask questions of chosen Unity Catalog data in natural language; as a supervisor tool it answers data questions, such as work-order history, and whose permissions it applies is verified per tool below.

Write tool descriptions as contracts: what the tool answers, what it must not be used for, and what it returns. For example, `stock_lookup: live on-hand quantity by part number and plant; not for recommended-spares lists`. Keep the list short: every added tool is another way to be wrong.

Which identity a tool call runs with, and whether a Genie Agent or a function sees the end user's own permissions, depends on the tool type; verify it in current documentation for each tool before relying on it. The Terraform provider v1.133.0 page for this resource carries a Public Beta badge. MLflow's `ToolCallCorrectness` scorer judges whether the tools called and their arguments were reasonable, and the evaluation module goes deeper on tool-call checks.

beats.recap: Autonomous tool selection answers more questions and adds a decision that must be evaluated.
beats.changeNote: Renamed the Genie tool in this beat to its current name, Genie Agent (formerly Genie space), following Databricks developer documentation (devhub commit 35f4745, Genie Agents page). Identifiers stay as the Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 spells them: the supervisor tool type is genie_space and the Genie API uses space IDs.

beats.title: A custom agent buys control and the whole test burden
beats.outcome: Decide when to write an agent in code and list what your team then owns.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-ai-platform-custom-concept|custom agent]] is your own code. MLflow's ResponsesAgent interface wraps logic written with any agent framework. Databricks developer documentation now recommends running it in a Databricks App and calls deploying it with the agent framework's deploy() to its own agent endpoint, after logging it with MLflow and registering it in Unity Catalog, a legacy path. You control every step: retrieval order, citation format, which tools exist and how each authenticates. Notice in the second state that the same control moves dependency updates, tests, tracing setup and evaluation from the platform's column into your team's.

samajh.text: Readymade kurta lo to size chart se kaam chal jaata hai: cutting, silai, finishing sab dukaan ne tay kar diya. Darzi se silwao to collar, jeb, lambai sab aapki marzi, par naap dena, trial pe jaana, alteration karwana bhi aapki zimmedari. Jab readymade fit ho jaaye, darzi ke paas jaana sirf shauk hai; jab fit na ho, tabhi darzi ka kharcha banta hai.
samajh.mapping: The readymade garment is an Agent Bricks agent with platform-decided internals; the tailor is a custom agent whose every choice, fitting and alteration is your team's work.
samajh.boundary: Unlike a garment, an agent keeps changing after delivery: models, documents and dependencies drift, so the custom path's testing and redeploying never ends.

handbook.markdown:
The custom path in code, with synthetic names:

```python
# agent.py (models-from-code), sketch only
import mlflow
from mlflow.pyfunc import ResponsesAgent
from mlflow.types.responses import ResponsesAgentRequest, ResponsesAgentResponse

class ManualsAgent(ResponsesAgent):
    def predict(self, request: ResponsesAgentRequest) -> ResponsesAgentResponse:
        question = request.input[-1].content     # latest user message, plain text assumed
        passages = retrieve(question)            # your retrieval and plant filter
        answer = generate(question, passages)    # your prompt and citation format
        return ResponsesAgentResponse(
            output=[self.create_text_output_item(text=answer, id="msg-1")]
        )

mlflow.models.set_model(ManualsAgent())
```

In MLflow 3.16.1, ResponsesAgent is the base class for agents that can wrap any framework, with `predict`, `predict_stream` and helpers for text and function-call items; MLflow recommends it over the older ChatAgent. The class and call above were run in this build against a local MLflow 3.16.1 with stub `retrieve` and `generate` functions and no model call. Logging, registration and `deploy()` are in the serving beat. Databricks developer documentation calls that deployment to a custom agent's own Model Serving endpoint a legacy path and recommends running the agent in a Databricks App instead.

Reasons Cinderline might choose this path: a retrieval order the platform does not offer (the newest revision of a manual first, then bulletins), a citation format with revision and page, a deterministic refusal when no passage passes a threshold, or a tool that must run as a specific service principal. Each is a requirement the Knowledge Assistant's configuration cannot express; confirm that against its current options before writing code.

What the team then owns: dependency pinning and updates, unit tests for retrieval and refusal, an evaluation set run on every change, the MLflow experiment for traces (deploy warns when none is found), redeploys (and, on the legacy endpoint path, removal of old served versions), and the response when an answer is wrong. Estimate that work before choosing; it is the price of control.

beats.recap: Code buys control over every step and makes every step your team's to test.
beats.changeNote: Corrected how this beat describes hosting a custom agent: it had taught deployment with the agent framework as the way one runs. Databricks developer documentation (devhub commit 35f4745, custom agents page) recommends a Databricks App and calls agents.deploy() to the agent's own endpoint a legacy path; the outcome, visual and list of owned work now mark which steps belong to that path.

beats.title: When one corpus answers the question, a fixed retrieval workflow wins
beats.outcome: Decide from a labelled question mix whether a fixed retrieve-then-answer workflow is enough or autonomous tool selection is needed.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-ai-platform-workflow-concept|fixed retrieval workflow]] always takes the same steps: retrieve passages the user may see, answer from them with citations, or say the manuals do not cover it. Its model calls, latency and failure points are countable in advance. Notice in the table that 46 of Cinderline's 60 labelled questions need only the manuals and 6 should be refused; [[dbxfe-ai-platform-autonomy-concept|autonomous tool selection]] would add a routing decision to all 60 to serve the 8 that need stock or history.

samajh.text: Railway enquiry counter aur travel agent ka farq socho. Enquiry counter sirf timetable dekh ke batata hai: kaunsi gaadi, kab, kis platform se. Har baar wahi kadam, jawab pakka. Travel agent khud decide karta hai: pehle ticket, phir hotel, phir cab. Woh zyada kaam kar sakta hai, par har decision mein galti ka mauka bhi hai. Agar sawal sirf timetable ka hai, travel agent bulana bekaar hai.
samajh.mapping: The enquiry counter is a fixed retrieval workflow over one corpus; the travel agent is autonomous tool selection that decides which bookings to make.
samajh.boundary: Unlike a timetable clerk, a retrieval workflow can still retrieve the wrong passage or answer badly; fixed steps make failures countable, not impossible.

handbook.markdown:
The choice is not between a simple system and a smart one; it is between fixed steps and chosen steps.

```text
Fixed retrieval workflow (every question)
  1. retrieve passages the user may see, filtered by plant
  2. if no passage passes the threshold: refuse and say why
  3. generate an answer from the passages, citing manual and revision

Autonomous tool selection (every question)
  1. decide which tools to call, from descriptions and instructions
  2. call one or more tools; handle refusals and errors
  3. generate an answer from whatever came back
```

Prefer the fixed workflow when one authoritative corpus answers most questions, when answers must be auditable (the same question takes the same path), when refusals must be predictable, and when cost and latency need forecasting. Move to tool selection when a material share of real questions needs a second source, when data must be live, or when requests genuinely vary in what they need. Write the threshold down before looking at results, as in the visual's third state.

Two cautions. A Knowledge Assistant is a managed retrieval agent: it is configured, not coded, and its internals may take more steps than the three above, but for this decision it sits on the retrieval side because it chooses no tools. And a fixed workflow is not automatically safe: permission filtering, stale documents and weak citations still fail, as the retrieval module shows.

What to inspect before deciding: the labelled mix, the share of questions one corpus answers, and, in traces from a pilot, how many steps each question actually took. Actions, such as drafting a work order, are a separate decision that needs its own authorization design before any agent may take them.

beats.recap: Start with fixed retrieval when one corpus answers most questions; write down what would justify tools.

beats.title: Choose with five criteria, not with the newest name
beats.outcome: Fill a decision table on customization, data access, operations, evaluation and risk for several supported patterns and defend the choice.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-ai-platform-decision-concept|decision table]] scores every candidate pattern on the same five criteria. Customization asks how much of the logic you can change; data access asks which sources and identities the pattern reaches; operations asks who deploys, updates and monitors it; evaluation asks how you will measure it before and after release; risk asks what fails and who is exposed. Notice in the last state that Cinderline picks the Knowledge Assistant because it meets the manuals-only requirement with the least owned code, not because of its age.

handbook.markdown:
Use the table in three passes.

1. **Filter** on hard constraints: data that may not leave Databricks, a release stage your security review will not accept, a region where the feature is unavailable. A pattern that fails a hard constraint is out, however well it reads elsewhere.
2. **Score** the rest on the five criteria, in words, as in the visual. Numbers invite false precision; a sentence per cell can be challenged.
3. **Name the switching condition**: the evidence that would move you to the next pattern.

| Pattern | Pick it when | Avoid it when |
|---|---|---|
| `ai_query` or a task function | The work is a column over a table | A person asks interactive questions |
| Fixed retrieval workflow (code) | You need exact steps and full control, or the managed agent is unavailable | The team cannot maintain code |
| Knowledge Assistant | Documents answer the questions and its configuration is enough | You need a custom retrieval order or format |
| Supervisor Agent | Questions genuinely need several tools | One corpus answers most questions |
| Custom agent (code) | Requirements exceed configuration and you can own the tests | A configured agent already meets them |

For Cinderline, the filter removes external models for manual content. The Knowledge Assistant meets the manuals requirement with the least owned code, so it leads; because its status in Cinderline's region is unverified, a fixed retrieval workflow in code is the named fallback; the Supervisor Agent waits for the switching condition.

The newest pattern is not a criterion. Newer managed patterns decide more for you, which is exactly right when their decisions match your requirements and exactly wrong when they do not. Say so in the design review, and bring the labelled question mix as the evidence. A table like this is also the easiest artifact to revisit: when a requirement changes, re-run the filter and the affected cells rather than the whole debate.

beats.recap: Filter on hard constraints, score five criteria in words, and name the switching condition.

beats.title: Hosting, governing and paying are three different owners
beats.outcome: Draw who hosts, who governs and who pays for each component of a managed AI design.
beats.explanation: In Cinderline's design, Databricks hosts the serving compute, the pay-per-token models and the Agent Bricks orchestration. Cinderline governs the data, the grants, the gateway settings and the evaluation, and pays Databricks for usage. If an external model were added, the provider would host that model and bill Cinderline's provider account. Notice in the diagram that [[dbxfe-ai-platform-responsibility-concept|governing and hosting]] sit with different parties, so a data-exposure failure is Cinderline's to fix even on fully managed compute.

samajh.text: Kiraye ke flat mein lift, paani ki tanki aur security society chalati hai. Par ghar ki chaabi kisko deni hai, almari mein kya rakhna hai, yeh aapka faisla hai. Kiraya aur bijli ka bill bhi aap bharte ho. Agar aapne padosi ko chaabi de di aur saaman gaayab hua, to society ki lift achhi chalne se kuch nahi badalta.
samajh.mapping: The society running the building is Databricks hosting serving compute; the keys and cupboard contents are Cinderline's grants and sources; rent and electricity are usage charges.
samajh.boundary: A platform's hosting duties are set by contracts and documentation rather than society bylaws, and an external provider adds a separate landlord with its own terms.

handbook.markdown:
A responsibilities table for Cinderline, in guidance terms rather than contract terms:

| Component | Hosts | Governs | Pays |
|---|---|---|---|
| Serving and agent endpoints | Databricks (serverless, outside Cinderline's cloud account) | Cinderline: CAN_QUERY, CAN_MANAGE, gateway settings | Cinderline, for usage |
| Pay-per-token or provisioned model | Databricks | Cinderline chooses model and mode | Cinderline, for tokens or capacity |
| External model | The provider | Cinderline: what may be sent; key in a secret scope | Cinderline, to the provider; any Databricks charge per current pricing |
| Knowledge sources | Cinderline's Unity Catalog storage | Cinderline: grants and document control | Cinderline, for storage and index |
| Agent Bricks orchestration | Databricks | Cinderline: configuration and permissions | Cinderline, for usage |
| Evaluation and sign-off | Cinderline's MLflow experiment | Cinderline | Cinderline, for judge-model calls |

The Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 states that serving endpoints and their compute are fully managed by Databricks and do not appear in the customer's cloud account; the Terraform provider v1.133.0 says endpoint tags are propagated to billing logs, which is how usage is attributed to a cost centre.

Use the table to route incidents. An answer revealing another plant's bulletin is a governance failure: the sources were scoped too widely, or permission-aware retrieval was assumed and never verified. A slow endpoint is a hosting or capacity question. An invoice surprise is a paying question that starts in the usage-tracking system tables. Contract terms, data-processing agreements and support boundaries are legal documents this table does not replace.

beats.recap: Managed hosting leaves governance and payment with the customer; an external model adds a third party.

beats.title: A release stage is a dated label on a named artifact
beats.outcome: Build an availability and status table whose filled cells name their artifact and date, and leave the other cells unknown.
beats.explanation: Terraform provider v1.133.0 pages label the Knowledge Assistant and Supervisor Agent resources Public Beta and the Unity Catalog model service GA, and say the provisioned-throughput endpoint resource is in private preview for enrolled customers. Each is a [[dbxfe-ai-platform-stage-concept|release stage]] label on one artifact on one date. None says whether Cinderline's cloud, region or workspace has the feature, and a service appearing in an SDK changelog is not a stage at all. Notice in the second state that most cells stay unknown until someone checks current documentation and the workspace.

handbook.markdown:
Three kinds of statement get confused.

**Release-stage labels.** The Terraform provider v1.133.0 pages carry badges that link to Databricks' release-types page: Public Beta on `databricks_knowledge_assistant` and `databricks_supervisor_agent`, GA on `databricks_ai_gateway_model_service`. The provisioned-throughput resource page instead says the resource is in private preview and only available for enrolled customers, a statement about that Terraform resource, not about provisioned throughput itself. The release-types page defines what each stage means for support and production use; read it for the stage you find rather than assuming a Beta or Preview label means almost-GA.

**Client-library dates.** The SDK changelog records `knowledge_assistants` arriving in v0.97.0 (2026-03-09), `supervisor_agents` in v0.105.0 (2026-04-23), the Unity Catalog `ai_gateway` in v0.123.0 (2026-07-30) and `ai_functions` in v0.134.0 (2026-09-03). These date the client, not the product. Package metadata is weaker still: databricks-agents 1.12.0 declares `Development Status :: 3 - Alpha`, a PyPI classifier, not a Databricks stage.

**Availability for you.** Cloud, region, workspace tier, enablement, and whether answers respect each user's permissions are properties of Cinderline's account. Verify them in the current documentation for Cinderline's cloud (the AWS, Azure and Google Cloud documentation sets are separate) and in the workspace itself.

A launch announcement is a lead. It can tell you what to look for; it cannot fill a region cell, prove parity across clouds or set a stage. Record every filled cell as value, artifact, date and who checked, and re-check before each design review, because labels move: the SDK and the Terraform page already disagree about AI Gateway support in the same week.

beats.recap: Fill a status cell only with a dated statement from a named artifact; leave the rest unknown.

beats.title: A cost estimate names its drivers and leaves prices to the day
beats.outcome: Write a cost-assumption table that multiplies synthetic volumes by named drivers and says check current pricing for every rate.
beats.explanation: Model costs follow drivers you can count: questions, tokens per question, model and tool calls per question, capacity hours for provisioned throughput, rows passed to an AI function, index hosting, and evaluation runs that call judge models. A [[dbxfe-ai-platform-cost-concept|cost assumption]] multiplies synthetic volumes by those drivers and leaves every rate as check current pricing. Notice in the equation that a supervisor's routing and tool calls multiply the calls per question before any price is applied.

handbook.markdown:
A cost note that survives review has three columns you can defend and one you refuse to guess.

```text
Cost assumption, Cinderline assistant (synthetic volumes)
component          driver                              volume            rate
answering model    input + output tokens x questions   300/day x 3,400   check current pricing
retrieval index    index hosting                       2,400 manuals     check current pricing
agent endpoint     compute while provisioned           1 endpoint        check current pricing
nightly labelling  rows x tokens per row               40,000 notes      check current pricing
evaluation         judge calls x rows x runs           60 x 4 x 10       check current pricing
```

Reason about multipliers before prices. Autonomous tool selection raises calls per question from two to three or four in the synthetic example. A join in front of `ai_query` can triple rows. A provisioned endpoint is charged for the capacity kept even when traffic is low, plus any burst capacity used under load (check how burst is billed). Old agent versions kept served at zero traffic, with scale-to-zero off by default in databricks-agents 1.12.0, can keep compute running. Evaluation is not free: every judge-based scorer is a model call per row per run.

Then replace assumptions with measurements. With the AI Gateway's usage tracking enabled, system tables record operational usage on endpoints and their associated costs; endpoint tags propagate to billing logs; a `client_request_id` sent with a query is recorded in the inference and usage-tracking tables, which lets you join usage to your own request log. Rates, currencies, discounts and regional differences are read from current pricing and the account's agreement on the day of the estimate, never from a course, a blog or memory.

beats.recap: Count the drivers and multiply the volumes; take every rate from current pricing on the day.

beats.title: Evaluate the alternatives on one labelled question set before choosing
beats.outcome: Plan an evaluation that runs every candidate pattern on the same labelled questions with scorers and human review, and keeps it running after release.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-ai-platform-evalset-concept|evaluation set]] holds labelled questions with expected facts, expected sources and expected refusals. Run the Knowledge Assistant and the fixed workflow on the same set with MLflow's evaluate and built-in scorers such as correctness, retrieval groundedness and safety, then have maintenance engineers review disagreements. Agent Bricks agents each carry an MLflow experiment, and agent endpoints log payloads to inference tables. Notice in the third state that the candidate with the higher average fails a refusal case and the other cites a superseded revision, so the agreed rules block both.

handbook.markdown:
Evaluation turns the decision table's evaluation column into evidence. A sketch with the MLflow 3.16.1 API and synthetic content:

```python
import mlflow
from mlflow.genai.scorers import Correctness, RetrievalGroundedness, Safety, Guidelines

eval_data = [
    {"inputs": {"question": "What torque for the spindle bolts on press line 4?",
                "caller": "tech-plant2"},
     "expectations": {"expected_facts": ["45 N·m", "manual PL4-M revision C"]}},
    {"inputs": {"question": "Show bulletin SB-201 for plant 3.",
                "caller": "tech-plant2"},
     "expectations": {"expected_response": "A refusal: the bulletin is not available to plant 2."}},
]

def ask_candidate(question: str, caller: str) -> str:
    # your client code: query with that caller's own credential
    return call_endpoint("cinderline-manuals-ka", question, as_user=caller)

mlflow.genai.evaluate(
    data=eval_data,
    predict_fn=ask_candidate,
    scorers=[Correctness(), RetrievalGroundedness(), Safety(),
             Guidelines(name="cites_revision",
                        guidelines="Cite the manual and its revision for every instruction.")],
)
```

`evaluate` passes each row's `inputs` to `predict_fn` as keyword arguments and returns metrics and per-row assessments. Every row carries its caller: a run under the app's or the evaluator's identity can neither pass nor fail a permission case such as SB-201. Correctness checks expected facts or an expected response; RetrievalGroundedness needs traces that record retrieval, which a remote endpoint call may not expose, so check what your traces contain; Guidelines checks your own written rule. The scorer objects above were constructed against a local MLflow 3.16.1 in this build; no judge model was called.

Plan it this way: collect 60 real technician questions, label expected facts, sources and refusals with a maintenance engineer, and add tool-call cases only if a supervisor is a candidate. Agree the rules before any run: every refusal case passes, no answer cites a superseded revision (the retrieval module's pass bar), correctness at or above a threshold, an engineer reviews every failure. Run each candidate on the same rows, then keep the set running after release on sampled production traffic from the agent endpoint's inference table and the agent's MLflow experiment. Judge scores are evidence to inspect, not verdicts; the evaluation module covers dataset design, judges and failure analysis in depth.

beats.recap: Run every candidate on one labelled set under rules agreed before the results.

extensionCards.prompt: What does the Unity Catalog AI Gateway service in SDK 0.141.0 govern that an endpoint's ai_gateway settings do not?
extensionCards.answer: Model services, model provider services and MCP services as Unity Catalog securables, with schema privileges, routing across destinations, rate limits and inference tables.
extensionCards.explanation: The SDK's catalog ai_gateway service, added to the client in v0.123.0, manages governed securables rather than settings on one endpoint. A [[dbxfe-ai-platform-extension-ucgateway-concept|model service]] routes requests to pay-per-token, provisioned-throughput or external destinations with fallback, rate limits and an inference table; creating one needs CREATE_SERVICE and USE_SCHEMA on the parent schema and EXECUTE on each referenced model or provider service. Model provider services hold external-provider credentials, and MCP services register MCP servers. The Terraform provider v1.133.0 labels the model service resource GA; confirm availability for your workspace, and do not confuse it with the endpoint-level configuration: in SDK 0.141.0 only the endpoint-level settings have guardrail fields.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Two surfaces share the AI Gateway name, so designs and reviews must say which one they mean.

extensionCards.prompt: How does the open-source MLflow AI Gateway differ from a Databricks serving endpoint's AI Gateway settings?
extensionCards.answer: The open-source one is a gateway server in the MLflow package that you host and operate; the Databricks settings are managed configuration on serving endpoints.
extensionCards.explanation: MLflow 3.16.1 ships a [[dbxfe-ai-platform-extension-mlflowgateway-concept|gateway server titled MLflow AI Gateway]], started from a configuration file on a host and port you choose; its start command is marked deprecated in favour of a newer UI-based AI Gateway in MLflow, and the package's gateway module includes budget and guardrail code. Whoever runs it hosts, secures and patches it. Databricks' AI Gateway settings on serving endpoints are configuration Databricks applies per endpoint, with results in Unity Catalog and system tables; Databricks developer documentation now lists them as the previous version of Unity AI Gateway, its governance layer for LLM endpoints and MCP servers. When a document or colleague says AI Gateway, ask which product, which version and who hosts it before comparing features.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Name collisions produce wrong feature comparisons; asking who hosts a component settles which one is meant.

extensionCards.prompt: What does the Custom LLM service, exposed as the SDK's agent_bricks service, keep and consume?
extensionCards.answer: A named custom LLM with instructions, guidelines, a serving endpoint name and Unity Catalog tables of request and optional response columns for training and evaluation.
extensionCards.explanation: In SDK 0.141.0 the agent_bricks service is described as managing state for the [[dbxfe-ai-platform-extension-customllm-concept|Custom LLM product]]. A custom LLM records instructions and guidelines, the endpoint that serves it, and datasets defined as Unity Catalog tables with a request column and, when labelled, a response column; the datasets are for training and evaluating the model, not for inference. Optimization can be started and cancelled and moves through states such as PENDING, RUNNING and COMPLETED. The client says nothing about what optimization changes, what it costs or where it is available, so those are verification items. For Cinderline it is a candidate only for a narrow, repeated text task with labelled examples, never for answering from manuals.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Agent Bricks is more than assistants; knowing each agent's inputs keeps a task-shaped need out of a chat assistant.

extensionCards.prompt: What happens to an agent's production traces when deploy() finds no MLflow experiment?
extensionCards.answer: databricks-agents 1.12.0 warns that traces from the deployment will not be logged in real time to MLflow or monitored.
extensionCards.explanation: In databricks-agents 1.12.0, deploy() looks for a tracing experiment in the endpoint's environment variables, then in the endpoint's existing monitor, then in the active MLflow experiment. If none is found it logs a warning that traces will not be logged in real time or monitored and asks for MLflow 3 or later with an experiment set through mlflow.set_experiment() before deploying. When one is found, it sets that [[dbxfe-ai-platform-extension-tracing-concept|tracing experiment]] in the endpoint's environment and tags the endpoint with it. Without traces, the post-release half of the evaluation plan has no production data to sample, so setting the experiment is a release checklist item, not a detail.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Post-release evaluation needs production traces, and a warning at deploy time is easy to miss.

recap.title: Choose the block by who writes the logic, then verify, cost and evaluate it
recap.markdown: **Managed AI on Databricks is a set of building blocks, each defined by who writes the logic above the model.** Model access (pay-per-token, provisioned throughput or external models), AI Functions in SQL, Agent Bricks agents such as the Knowledge Assistant and the Supervisor Agent, and custom agents in code, which Databricks developer documentation now recommends running in a Databricks App rather than deploying to their own endpoint, all reach models through serving endpoints; the AI Gateway governs those endpoints, although which of its features apply depends on the endpoint type, and MLflow evaluates whatever you build. Choose with five criteria, not novelty; prefer a fixed retrieval workflow when one corpus answers most questions; say who hosts, governs and pays; fill status cells only from dated, named artifacts; and leave every rate to current pricing. **Transfer challenge:** for a hospital pharmacy's formulary assistant that must also check live stock of a medicine, rebuild the decision, status and cost tables and write the evaluation rule that would block release.

appliedTask.title: Re-decide when stock questions grow
appliedTask.prompt: Six months after launch, Cinderline's second plant joins. Its technicians' labelled questions are 30 from manuals, 14 needing live spare-part stock, 6 needing work-order history and 5 that should be refused; they also ask the assistant to draft, not submit, work orders. Security's rule on manuals is unchanged, and the Supervisor Agent's status in the region is still unverified. Decide the pattern for plant 2, the controls, the evaluation changes and what you mark unknown.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Stock and history now reach 20 of 55 questions, above the one-in-five switching condition, so pilot a Supervisor Agent with three tools: the existing manuals Knowledge Assistant, a stock_lookup Unity Catalog function and a work-order Genie Agent (the genie_space tool type), each with a contract-style description. Drafting a work order is an action: keep it out until an authorization design exists and link to the maintenance system instead. Keep Databricks-hosted models only. Put rate limits and guardrails on the model endpoints, because SDK 0.141.0 says agent endpoints support only inference tables, and grant EXECUTE on stock_lookup to the identity the tool runs as. Extend the evaluation set with tool-call cases, two-part questions and denied-tool runs, agree the rules first and keep plant 1's set as a regression check. Keep the fixed retrieval workflow as the fallback if the supervisor cannot be verified. Mark unknown: the supervisor's release stage and regional availability, which identity each tool runs with, and every price.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer applies the switching condition written at launch, separates answering from acting, places each control on a layer that supports it, and turns every availability and identity question into a verification item instead of an assumption.
